subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Companion cells are essential to phloem transport because they:
options: Store starch for the sieve tubes
Contain no organelles, reducing resistance to flow
Provide ATP and actively load sucrose into the sieve tube elements
Conduct water under tension like xylem vessels
questions.explain: Companion cells, rich in mitochondria, actively load sucrose into sieve tubes at the source, driving mass flow.

questions.q: Glucose is absorbed across the ileum epithelium into the blood by:
options: Co-transport with sodium ions, the Na+ gradient being maintained by a sodium-potassium pump
Active transport directly using ATP at the apical membrane
Simple diffusion only, down its concentration gradient
Facilitated diffusion at the apical membrane independent of sodium
questions.explain: Na+/glucose co-transporters move glucose against its gradient using the Na+ gradient set up by the Na+/K+ pump on the basal membrane.

questions.q: Fetal haemoglobin has a dissociation curve to the LEFT of adult haemoglobin because:
options: It has a higher affinity for oxygen, allowing it to load oxygen from maternal blood at the placenta
It carries less oxygen overall
It must release oxygen more readily to the placenta
It is less saturated at every partial pressure of oxygen
questions.explain: A higher oxygen affinity (curve to the left) lets fetal Hb take up oxygen from maternal Hb across the placenta.

questions.q: Insects limit water loss from their tracheal system mainly by:
options: Closing the spiracles using valves and hairs
Increasing ventilation by abdominal pumping
Producing surfactant in the tracheoles
Using haemoglobin to carry oxygen in the blood
questions.explain: Spiracles can be closed by valves, reducing the evaporative water loss that would otherwise occur from the moist tracheal lining.

questions.q: A waxy cuticle on the upper surface of a leaf is an adaptation that:
options: Reduces water loss by evaporation through the upper epidermis
Allows more carbon dioxide to diffuse inward
Increases the rate of transpiration
Provides the main site of gas exchange
questions.explain: The waterproof waxy cuticle limits evaporative water loss from the leaf surface, conserving water.

questions.q: During inspiration in a mammal, the pressure in the thorax falls because:
options: The volume of the thoracic cavity increases as the diaphragm flattens and the ribs move up and out
The diaphragm relaxes and domes upward
The external intercostal muscles relax
Surfactant reduces the surface tension of the alveoli
questions.explain: Contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostals increases thoracic volume, lowering pressure below atmospheric so air flows in.

questions.q: Compared with elastic recoil in expiration, why are the walls of arteries elastic?
options: To stretch under high pressure and recoil, smoothing out pressure surges and maintaining flow
To enable exchange of materials with tissues
To allow active contraction that pumps blood
To slow blood flow for absorption
questions.explain: Elastic tissue in artery walls stretches during systole and recoils during diastole, evening out pulsatile pressure and sustaining blood flow.

questions.q: As an organism increases in size, why does it require a specialised exchange surface?
options: Its surface-area-to-volume ratio increases, slowing diffusion
Volume increases more slowly than surface area
Larger cells respire anaerobically and need no oxygen
Its surface-area-to-volume ratio decreases, so diffusion across the body surface cannot meet metabolic demand
questions.explain: As size increases, volume rises faster than surface area, so the SA:V ratio falls and the body surface alone cannot supply the cells.

questions.q: Why is the tracheal system of an insect generally unsuitable for supporting a very large body size?
options: Diffusion of oxygen along long tracheae becomes too slow to meet demand deep in the body
Haemolymph cannot carry any oxygen
Spiracles cannot be closed in large insects
Tracheoles fill permanently with fluid in large insects
questions.explain: Because the system relies largely on diffusion, oxygen cannot reach deep tissues fast enough in a large insect, limiting body size.

questions.q: Most tissue fluid is returned to the circulation by the:
options: Active transport across the capillary wall
Arteriole end of the capillary
Venule end of the capillary only, driven by osmosis
Combination of osmotic return at the venule end and drainage by the lymphatic system
questions.explain: Some fluid re-enters at the venule end down a water-potential gradient, and the excess is collected and returned by the lymphatic system.

questions.q: A potometer measures the rate of water uptake by a shoot, which is used as an estimate of transpiration. A key assumption is that:
options: Stomata are fully closed throughout
Water uptake exactly equals water lost as vapour
The shoot continues to grow during the experiment
No water is used in photosynthesis or stored in cells
questions.explain: The potometer assumes that virtually all water taken up is lost in transpiration, though a small amount is actually used by the plant.

questions.q: In the cohesion-tension theory of water transport, water moves up the xylem because:
options: Transpiration creates tension, and cohesion between water molecules pulls a continuous column upward
Root pressure alone is sufficient in tall trees
Active transport pumps water from root to leaf
Osmosis pushes water from the leaves down to the roots
questions.explain: Evaporation from leaves lowers pressure, and hydrogen-bonded cohesion lets a continuous water column be pulled up under tension.

questions.q: In the ileum epithelial cell, the sodium-potassium pump that maintains glucose co-transport is located in the:
options: Membrane of the mitochondria
Basolateral membrane facing the blood
Apical (microvillus) membrane facing the lumen
Nuclear membrane
questions.explain: The Na+/K+ pump sits on the basolateral membrane, pumping Na+ into the blood to keep intracellular Na+ low so apical co-transport continues.

questions.q: Why does a single circulatory system (as in fish) deliver blood to the body at a lower pressure than a double system?
options: Fish have no heart
Blood passes through the gill capillaries before reaching the body, so pressure drops before systemic delivery
Fish blood is more viscous
The heart has four chambers in fish
questions.explain: In a single circuit blood loses pressure passing through the gill capillaries, so it reaches the body more slowly than in a double system.

questions.q: Tissue fluid is formed at the arteriole end of a capillary mainly because:
options: Plasma proteins leave the capillary
Hydrostatic (blood) pressure exceeds the oncotic pull of plasma proteins, forcing fluid out
The low water potential of the blood draws water out
Oncotic pressure exceeds hydrostatic pressure
questions.explain: At the arteriole end high hydrostatic pressure outweighs the water potential gradient created by plasma proteins, so fluid is forced out.

questions.q: Which adaptation of the alveolar epithelium most directly reduces the diffusion distance for gases?
options: Squamous (flattened) epithelial cells forming a wall one cell thick
A rich capillary network surrounding each alveolus
A large total surface area provided by millions of alveoli
Surfactant lining the alveolar surface
questions.explain: Flattened squamous cells make the alveolar wall extremely thin, minimising the distance gases must diffuse.

questions.q: In bony fish, the operculum contributes to gas exchange by:
options: Adding oxygen to the water before it reaches the gills
Maintaining a near-continuous flow of water over the gills
Pumping blood through the gill lamellae
Filtering food particles from the water
questions.explain: Coordinated movements of the buccal cavity and operculum keep water flowing over the gills almost continuously, maintaining exchange.

questions.q: At high altitude, where the partial pressure of oxygen is low, the oxygen dissociation curve of a well-adapted animal is often shifted to the LEFT because:
options: Haemoglobin must release oxygen more readily to tissues
Carbon dioxide levels are always higher at altitude
Tissues require less oxygen at altitude
A higher oxygen affinity helps haemoglobin load oxygen at the low oxygen partial pressures found there
questions.explain: A leftward shift (higher affinity) allows haemoglobin to become saturated despite the low oxygen partial pressure of high-altitude air.

questions.q: The very large surface area of the small intestine for absorption is produced by:
options: Numerous goblet cells secreting mucus
Villi and microvilli on the epithelial cells
A dense capillary network in the submucosa only
A thick muscular wall
questions.explain: Folded villi each covered in microvilli (the brush border) massively increase the absorptive surface area of the ileum.

questions.q: During strenuous activity an insect may ventilate its tracheal system more effectively by:
options: Rhythmic abdominal pumping movements that move air through the tracheae
Increasing the water content of the tracheoles
Closing all spiracles to retain oxygen
Switching to cutaneous gas exchange
questions.explain: Abdominal muscle contractions change body volume, mass-flowing air through the tracheae to supplement diffusion during high demand.

questions.q: Carbon dioxide is mostly transported in the blood as:
options: Dissolved CO2 in the plasma
Carbonic acid in the plasma
Carbaminohaemoglobin
Hydrogencarbonate ions formed in red blood cells
questions.explain: Most CO2 is converted by carbonic anhydrase in red cells to carbonic acid, which dissociates into hydrogencarbonate ions carried in the plasma.

questions.q: The myoglobin dissociation curve lies to the LEFT of the haemoglobin curve, which means myoglobin:
options: Cannot bind oxygen at low partial pressures
Carries four oxygen molecules like haemoglobin
Releases oxygen at higher partial pressures than haemoglobin
Has a higher affinity for oxygen and acts as an oxygen store in muscle
questions.explain: Myoglobin's high oxygen affinity means it only releases oxygen at very low partial pressures, acting as a reserve store in muscle.

questions.q: The sino-atrial node (SAN) is described as the pacemaker of the heart because it:
options: Initiates waves of excitation that set the basic heart rate
Prevents the atria and ventricles from contracting together
Conducts the impulse to the ventricles after a delay
Receives blood from the vena cava
questions.explain: The SAN spontaneously generates waves of depolarisation that spread across the atria and set the heart's intrinsic rhythm.

questions.q: In phloem, the mass-flow hypothesis explains translocation as a result of:
options: Diffusion of sucrose from source to sink
Cohesion-tension pulling sap upward
Capillary action in the sieve tubes
Active loading of sucrose at the source lowering water potential, drawing in water and raising hydrostatic pressure that drives flow to the sink
questions.explain: Sucrose loaded at the source lowers water potential so water enters by osmosis, raising pressure and forcing sap toward sinks where sucrose is unloaded.

questions.q: Guard cells open the stomata when they:
options: Are exposed to darkness
Lose potassium ions to neighbouring cells
Lose water and become flaccid
Accumulate solutes, take up water by osmosis and become turgid
questions.explain: Active uptake of K+ lowers guard-cell water potential, so water enters by osmosis; the cells become turgid and bend apart, opening the pore.

questions.q: Which factor would DECREASE the rate of transpiration from a leaf?
options: A decrease in atmospheric humidity
An increase in air movement (wind)
A rise in temperature
An increase in atmospheric humidity
questions.explain: Higher humidity reduces the water-potential gradient between the leaf air spaces and the atmosphere, slowing diffusion of water vapour out.

questions.q: Spongy mesophyll in a leaf is adapted for gas exchange because:
options: It transports water to the stomata
It actively pumps carbon dioxide into the cells
Air spaces between loosely packed cells provide a large moist surface for diffusion
It contains many chloroplasts for trapping light
questions.explain: Loosely packed cells with interconnected air spaces give a large moist surface area, allowing gases to diffuse to and from photosynthesising cells.

questions.q: What is the function of the non-conducting (fibrous) tissue between the atria and ventricles?
options: To speed conduction directly from atria to ventricles
To prevent blood entering the ventricles
To delay and channel the impulse through the AVN so the ventricles contract after the atria
To act as a second pacemaker
questions.explain: The fibrous ring stops the impulse passing directly to the ventricles, forcing it through the AVN, ensuring atria empty before ventricles contract.

questions.q: The semilunar (aortic and pulmonary) valves open when:
options: Ventricular pressure exceeds the pressure in the aorta and pulmonary artery
The AV valves are also open
Atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure
The ventricles relax during diastole
questions.explain: Once ventricular pressure rises above arterial pressure the semilunar valves open and blood is ejected.

questions.q: The Bohr effect describes how an increase in carbon dioxide (and fall in pH):
options: Has no effect on oxygen affinity
Shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the left, increasing haemoglobin's affinity
Increases the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood
Shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right, so haemoglobin releases more oxygen at a given partial pressure
questions.explain: Higher CO2 lowers haemoglobin's oxygen affinity, shifting the curve right so more oxygen is unloaded in respiring tissues.
